new_statements.quote: The Bantu words are invariably accented on the penultimate (next to the last) syllable. There is tone in a two-register system, but for the most part it seems to be of lexical importance only ... The Sudanic languages in the Ubangi, on the other hand, consist basically of monosyllabic words, that is, most of their "words" in simplest form consist of one syllable. They make very little use of affixation. In fact, the Ngbandi language, judging from my present analysis, will probably have no elements which need be considered as prefixes or suffixes. Accent or stress does not exist. The tonal system is extremely well developed, there being three registers of tone plus glides.

new_statements.rule_in_words: For the 'Sudanic' (Ubangian) languages of the Belgian-Congo Ubangi -- Ngbaka, Banda (whose largest dialect is Mbanza) and Ngbandi -- the author asserts there is no word accent or stress at all; prominence is purely tonal (three level tones plus glides), in contrast to the penultimate accent of the neighbouring Bantu languages and Lingala.
new_statements.domain_note: Areal, impressionistic generalisation in a missionary article whose own data are Ngbandi; Mbanza/Banda is covered only by inclusion in 'the Sudanic languages in the Ubangi' (enumerated p.40). Not a Mbandja-specific phonological analysis; word-level claim, no phrase-level discussion. The only other prosodic remarks touching Mbandja found: Mortier 1940 marks three tones and open syllables only (no stress remark); Tucker & Bryan 1966 sec. 2 'Tone and Stress' cite Mortier for a vowel-less tone in MBANJA and note for BANDA generally (Togbo-based) a 'tendency towards extra shortness' of the penultimate, without any stress-placement rule; Cloarec-Heiss 1978 (snippets) gives mbanza/mbanja segment inventories and 'un système tonal à trois registres' only.
new_statements.identity_note: Nelson 1952's 'no accent or stress' sentence is an areal claim about 'the Sudanic languages in the Ubangi' (Ngbaka, Banda, Ngbandi) from a Ngbandi fieldworker; Mbanza enters only as 'the largest dialect' of his Banda group (p.40). The inaccessible primary descriptions differ in variety: Tingbo 1978 describes the Báláwo dialect of Mbandza (DRC); Cloarec-Heiss 1978 separates 'mbanza (de Mongoumba)' (CAR/Congo border) from 'mbänjä (de Bujala [Budjala], Zaïre)', both falling under Glottolog mban1263 (Ethnologue dialects Gbado, Kala). Beware homonyms in searches: 'Mbandja' is also an Angolan Wambo (Kwanyama-related) variety and the name of the Gabonese Bwiti temple.

sources.locator: p. 41 (scope defined p. 40: 'The Banda language group is composed of six dialects: Mbanza, Ngbundu, Mono, Gobu, Togbo, and Langbase. The Mbanza is the largest dialect.')
sources.note: p.40 lists the Banda group of the Belgian-Congo Ubangi as six dialects 'Mbanza, Ngbundu, Mono, Gobu, Togbo, and Langbase. The Mbanza is the largest dialect.' p.41, contrasting Bantu (penultimate accent) with 'the Sudanic languages in the Ubangi' (Ngbaka, Banda, Ngbandi): 'Accent or stress does not exist. The tonal system is extremely well developed, there being three registers of tone plus glides.' Areal generalisation by a missionary whose own analysis is of Ngbandi; not a Mbandja-specific description.
